title: Sound check
description: «Sound check» – das vierte Modul im Englisch-Lernpfad «Cate's Sound Lab», für beide Züge: Hier wird gehört! Du verstehst kurze vorgelesene Sätze und einen kleinen Konzertbericht, ordnest Instrumente ihren Bildern und Adjektive ihren Übersetzungen zu, lernst den Unterschied zwischen so und such – und festigst das past perfect aus Modul 2. Niveau A2–B1 (9. Schulstufe).
subject: E
einheit: Cate's Sound Lab – über Musik sprechen
learningObjectives: I can understand short spoken sentences and a short spoken text about music. (Ich kann kurze gesprochene Sätze und einen kurzen gesprochenen Text über Musik verstehen.)
I can use so and such correctly. (Ich kann so und such richtig verwenden.)
I can use the music words from Module 1 and the past perfect from Module 2 again. (Ich kann den Wortschatz aus Modul 1 und das past perfect aus Modul 2 wieder anwenden.)

competencies.description: FS1E.1.A.1 (LiLe, Englisch 1. Fremdsprache – Hören): Die Schülerinnen und Schüler können verschiedenartige Hörtexte und Gespräche verstehen (Sachtexte, ästhetische Texte, Texte im Schulalltag, Gespräche im Kontakt mit Englisch sprechenden Personen).
FS1E.5.B.1 (LiLe – Sprache(n) im Fokus, Wortschatz): Die Schülerinnen und Schüler verfügen über einen angemessenen Wortschatz, um sich mündlich und schriftlich zu äussern.

FS1E.5.D.1 (LiLe – Sprache(n) im Fokus, Grammatik): Die Schülerinnen und Schüler können grammatische Strukturen in Texten erkennen und für das Verständnis nutzen sowie beim Sprechen und Schreiben anwenden.

blocks.title: Welcome to «Sound check»!
blocks.body:
Put your headphones on – this is a sound check! In the first three modules you read, wrote and built sentences. In this module, for the first time, you **listen**: your device reads short English sentences and a little story to you.

In this module you will:

- listen to short sentences and show what you heard,
- match instruments to pictures and adjectives to their German translations,
- learn the difference between the two small words **so** and **such**,
- listen to a short story about a festival evening – and use your past-tense knowledge from Week 1.

A tip before you start: you can play each audio clip as often as you like. If your device has no English voice, the text appears on the screen instead – then simply read it.

blocks.credit: Eigenaufnahme EveryCate (synthetische Stimme «Daniel», macOS), CC BY-SA 4.0
blocks.title: Warm-up sentence 1
blocks.vorleseText: The audience claps and sings along to the catchy chorus.
blocks.description: Press play and listen carefully. You can listen more than once. Then answer the question below.

options.text: The audience laughs and sings along to the catchy chorus.
The audience claps and sings along to the catchy chorus.
The audience claps and dances along to the catchy chorus.

questions.explanation: The sentence was: «The audience claps and sings along to the catchy chorus.» The audience claps (not laughs) and sings (not dances) – small differences, big listening practice!

blocks.credit: Eigenaufnahme EveryCate (synthetische Stimme «Daniel», macOS), CC BY-SA 4.0
blocks.title: Warm-up sentence 2
blocks.vorleseText: The drummer plays a powerful rhythm on the drums.
blocks.description: Listen again – this time there is a question about the meaning.

questions.prompt: Which instrument did you hear about?

options.text: The drums
The keyboard
The guitar
The microphone

questions.explanation: The sentence was: «The drummer plays a powerful rhythm on the drums.» A drummer plays the drums – and *powerful* is one of your adjectives from Module 1.

blocks.credit: Eigenaufnahme EveryCate (synthetische Stimme «Daniel», macOS), CC BY-SA 4.0
blocks.title: Warm-up sentence 3
blocks.vorleseText: Our school choir sings a relaxing melody in the hall.
blocks.description: Listen carefully – three very similar sentences will follow.

options.text: Our school choir sings a cheerful melody in the hall.
Our school band plays a relaxing melody in the hall.
Our school choir sings a relaxing melody in the hall.

questions.explanation: The sentence was: «Our school choir sings a relaxing melody in the hall.» It was the choir (a group of singers), and the melody was relaxing, not cheerful.

blocks.credit: Eigenaufnahme EveryCate (synthetische Stimme «Daniel», macOS), CC BY-SA 4.0
blocks.title: Warm-up sentence 4
blocks.vorleseText: The singer walks on stage and the lights go out.
blocks.description: One more sentence – then a question about what happens.

options.text: The singer leaves the stage.
The singer walks on stage.
The singer looks at the audience.
The singer starts to sing.

questions.explanation: The sentence was: «The singer walks on stage and the lights go out.» The singer walks ON stage – the show is about to begin. Singing is not mentioned yet!

blocks.title: Match B: Adjectives and their German translations
blocks.intro: Do you remember the describing words from Module 1? Match each English adjective to its German translation.

blocks.title: Language focus: so or such?
blocks.body:
Both words make things stronger – but they have different partners.

**so + adjective (or adverb)** – no noun after it:

- The melody is **so** catchy!
- The band played **so** loudly that the walls shook.

**such (+ a/an) + noun** – there is always a noun at the end, often with an adjective before it:

- It was **such a** great concert.
- They are **such** good musicians. *(plural – no a/an)*

**so many / so much** – before nouns you can or cannot count:

- There were **so many** fans in front of the arena. *(fans – you can count them)*
- The neighbours complained about **so much** noise. *(noise – you cannot count it)*

**Remember:** adjective alone → *so* · noun at the end → *such (a/an)* · plural you can count → *so many* · things you cannot count → *so much*. The picture below shows it in two columns.

blocks.title: so or such – the quick rule
blocks.alt: Memory chart with two columns. Left column, blue, titled «so»: so + adjective or adverb, with the examples «so catchy» and «so loudly». Right column, orange, titled «such»: such (+ a/an) + noun, with the examples «such a great concert» and «such good musicians». A dark bar at the bottom adds: so many + things you can count (so many fans) · so much + things you cannot count (so much noise).
blocks.caption: Adjective alone? Use so. A noun at the end? Use such.

blocks.title: Exercise: so, such and friends
blocks.intro: Drag the right words into the gaps (on a phone: tap first the word, then the gap). **Careful: two forms in the list are wrong forms – they fit nowhere.**
blocks.text:
The concert was {{1}} loud that my ears hurt the next day.
I had never heard {{2}} beautiful melody before.
There were {{3}} people in front of the stage that we could not see the band.
The crew has {{4}} to do before the show that nobody takes a break.
It was {{5}} unforgettable evening that we still talk about it.
They are {{6}} good musicians that every hall is full.

blocks.title: Exercise: Type so or such (a)
blocks.intro: Now without a word list: type **so**, **such** or **such a** into each gap. Look at what comes after the gap – an adjective alone, or a noun at the end?
blocks.text:
This song is {{1}} catchy that I hum it all day.
I had never been to {{2}} big concert before.
The tickets were {{3}} expensive that we stayed at home.
She is {{4}} talented singer that everyone wants a photo with her.
Why are you {{5}} nervous? It is only a sound check!

blocks.credit: Eigenaufnahme EveryCate (synthetische Stimme «Daniel», macOS), CC BY-SA 4.0
blocks.title: Listening: My first festival
blocks.vorleseText: Last Saturday, my brother took me to my first festival. When we arrived at the field, the first band had already played its last song. I was sad, because I had waited weeks for that band. But then the next group started – and it was such a powerful show that I forgot everything else.
blocks.description: Now a whole story! Listen as often as you like, then answer the three questions below. Tip: listen once for the whole story, and a second time for the details.

blocks.title: Check your listening: the festival story
blocks.intro: Three questions about the story you just heard. You can go back and listen again before you answer.

options.text: The speaker arrived at the field.
The first band played its last song.
Both happened at the same time.
The story does not say.

questions.explanation: You heard: «When we arrived at the field, the first band had already played its last song.» *Had played* is the past perfect from Week 1 – the tense for the earlier action. So the band finished first, and the speaker arrived too late.

questions.prompt: Why was the speaker sad at first?

options.text: The tickets for the festival had been much too expensive for the speaker.
The speaker's brother wanted to go home early because he was tired.
The speaker had waited weeks for the first band – and missed it.
The next group played so badly that everybody left the field.

questions.explanation: You heard: «I was sad, because I had waited weeks for that band.» The speaker had waited a long time for exactly that band – and arrived after its last song. The story says nothing about ticket prices, and the next group was great.

options.text: The next group played such a powerful show that the speaker forgot everything else.
The speaker was so sad that they went home before the next group started.
The show of the next group was so quiet and boring that almost everybody left.
The story does not tell us anything about how the festival evening ended.

questions.explanation: You heard: «It was such a powerful show that I forgot everything else.» A happy ending – with *such a* + adjective + noun, exactly the pattern from this module.

blocks.title: Quick repeat: past simple or past perfect?
blocks.intro: One last look back at Week 1: put the verb in brackets into the past simple or the past perfect.
blocks.text:
By the time the singer arrived, the fans {{1}} (wait) for three hours.
Everybody knew the lyrics, because the song {{2}} (be) number one for weeks before.
We {{3}} (buy) our tickets months before, so we walked straight in.
After the encore, we {{4}} (take) the bus home.

blocks.credit: Eigenaufnahme EveryCate (synthetische Stimme «Daniel», macOS), CC BY-SA 4.0
blocks.title: Final listening sentence
blocks.vorleseText: We had never seen such an amazing light show before.
blocks.description: One last sentence for your ears – the first question of the final quiz is about it.

blocks.title: Final quiz: ears, words and tenses
blocks.intro: Five questions from the whole module. For the first one, use the audio sentence above – you can play it again.

options.text: We had never seen such an amazing light show before.
We had never heard such an amazing light show before.
We have never seen such an amazing light show before.

questions.explanation: The sentence was: «We had never seen such an amazing light show before.» You *see* a light show (eyes, not ears!), and *had never seen* is the past perfect – the sentence looks back from a moment in the past.

options.text: stage
choir
lyrics
audience

questions.explanation: The audience is the group of people who watch and listen to a show – das Publikum. The stage is the Bühne, a choir is a Chor, and the lyrics are the Songtext.

questions.prompt: «I have never heard ___ boring song!» – What fits into the gap?

options.text: so
such a
so much
such

questions.explanation: At the end there is a noun (*song*) with an adjective before it – so you need *such a*: «such a boring song». *So* would need the adjective alone, *so much* only works with things you cannot count, and *such* without *a* only fits plurals or uncountable nouns – *song* is a single countable noun.

questions.prompt: «When the show ended, most fans ___ their voices from singing along.» – Which form fills the gap?

options.text: had lost
have lost
had lose
lose

questions.explanation: The singing (and the losing of voices) happened before the end of the show – the earlier action takes the past perfect: *had lost*. *Had lose* is the wrong form, and *have lost / lose* do not fit a story about the past.

options.text: It was so long sound check.
It was such long sound check.
It was such a long sound check.
It was so a long sound check.

questions.explanation: *Sound check* is a singular noun, so you need *such a*: «such a long sound check». *So* never takes a noun, and *such* without *a* only works with plurals or things you cannot count.
